Environment Watch

Two stations stand 28 m apart on the north-east highland, wired to the same alarm bus: a 10 m lattice mast that measures the air, and a Timepix4 particle camera that measures what comes through it. A net of silicon-carbide sentinels covers the rest of the depth axis — a trio on the fusion perimeter, one thirty metres down, one at three kilometres. When a storm arrives they all report, and the most informative report comes from the deepest one, which stays silent.

01

The alert cluster

Not a science site — an operations tripwire. Everything here exists because something else in the city has to stop when a number crosses a line.

The weather mast at (300, −300) carries three-level hot-film anemometry, a barometer enclosure, an air-temperature shield stack and a sun-tracking photometer. The photometer is the point: it measures dust optical depth τ, and τ is what the rest of the city subscribes to. Past τ = 3 the direct solar beam is down to 2.7% and the greenhouse dome switches its light budget to LEDs; the same threshold grounds the scout helicopter and freezes outdoor lifting. Three remote poles scattered 1.5–2.2 km out turn a single reading into a vector — where the front is coming from, and how many minutes are left.

The radiation station 28 m away answers a different question with the same urgency. Its Timepix4 camera records every particle as a track, and classifies by track shape rather than by energy: electrons curl, protons run straight, heavy ions burn short and bright. A solar particle event announces itself as a change in the picture, not in a single scalar. Both stations drive the same red lamp.

The city also runs a spectral tier — thermal-IR, UV and terahertz sounding stations that profile temperature, ozone and water vapour rather than raising alarms. Those live on The Spectrum Net.

02

One storm, three depths

The same event, read by instruments separated by kilometres of rock. The differences between their readings are the city's shielding calculation, measured live.

When a solar particle event reaches Mars, the surface camera's screen changes character within a minute: the sparse mix of curls and bars becomes a downpour of orange proton tracks, and the alarm tower steps from green to red. The trigger is deliberately dumb — a one-minute sliding count, green below 3× quiet, red above 30×. Quiet-rate Poisson noise is about 1.6% per minute, so even the low threshold sits more than 20σ out; false alarms are not the failure mode worth engineering against.

Thirty metres down, in the undercity foyer, the same event is nearly invisible. Rock annihilates the hadronic component — 30 m is 7800 g/cm², about 52 hadronic e-foldings — and what still trickles through is almost pure muon flux, ×0.03 of the surface value. On an 8 cm² sentinel that is one count every 83 seconds, storm or no storm.

At 3 km, the deep-lab sentinel does not respond at all. Muons are down by another factor of 3×10⁻⁵ and the neutron background has fallen to the bare rock's own U/Th (α,n) floor. Combined, that is roughly one count every 26 days. The instrument's job there is to be boring: the dark-matter experiment above it stakes a 70 t·yr exposure on the premise that this column is quiet, and this is the column that checks the premise.

Surface · fusion fence
2.32 counts/s

A blip about every 0.43 s — roughly 1400× the ambient GCR neutron floor (re-anchored 2026-09-02 to the declared 0.30 m bio-shield; the earlier 0.21 → 0.08 counts/s and 12 s cadence sat behind a self-assumed 2 m shield). This one is not listening for space weather at all; it watches 14 MeV leakage through the tokamak's breeding blanket.

−30 m · undercity foyer
83 s per count

Hadrons are gone after 52 e-foldings of rock. What still ticks is the muon residual — the shallow tier's occasional blip is almost pure µ.

−3000 m · deep lab
26 days per count

Muons ×10⁻⁶, neutrons at the radiogenic limit. Proof by silence: if this column ever starts ticking rhythmically, the cavern background has gone wrong.

Why tiers instead of one good detector. Each sentinel measures the transmission of the matter column directly above it, so the ratios between tiers are the measured attenuation of each rock section. The city ends up with its own depth-intensity calibration rather than a handbook value — and the same four-decade span is why no single detector could have done it.

03

How they work

Five instruments worth the detail — three on the mast, two underground — because in each case the obvious terrestrial answer fails outright at 610 Pa, or next to a fusion plant, or under three kilometres of rock.

WindWhy the big cups are decoration

Martian dynamic pressure is 83× below Earth's: a 30 m/s gale carries 6.6 Pa, the same push as a 3.3 m/s breeze at home. An Earth-standard cup set (7 cm cups, 15 cm arms) would not start turning until 3.44 m/s, missing most of the wind spectrum. The oversized display cups on the masthead start at 0.79 m/s — honest, just slow. The real measurement is made by hot films, as on Perseverance's MEDA.

A film left to itself is useless here: its open-loop thermal time constant is 17–48 s, so constant-power heating cannot follow even a 0.01 Hz fluctuation. The instrument is the servo. A constant-overheat bridge pins the film's resistance — hence its temperature — and whatever heat the wind steals, the bridge instantly resupplies; the resupply power is the measurement. That collapses the effective time constant by a factor of ~925 to 29.5 ms (f₃dB 5.4 Hz), which finally covers the 0.1–3 Hz gust band. Three films at 120° resolve direction to 1.4–1.8° — two would leave a mirror ambiguity, three is the minimal unique solver.

PressureA buffer volume with a cutoff frequency

The barometer is a vacuum-referenced silicon capsule, and its geometry is set by one collision: the first 18 µm diaphragm deflected 6.2 µm at full scale and would have bottomed out on a 2 µm capacitive gap. Deflection scales as 1/t³, so the shipping part is 40 µm and moves 0.56 µm — 0.1 Pa maps to 10.4 ppm of capacitance, comfortably inside a commodity converter. The intake is not a hole but a filter: pipe resistance times buffer-volume compliance forms a first-order low-pass at 1.39 Hz, deliberately placed so thermal tides and dust-devil transients pass while wind-turbulence noise does not.

Optical depthCalibration you have to earn

τ comes from Beer–Lambert extinction of the direct solar beam at 880 nm, which requires knowing the unattenuated intensity I₀ — and there is no standard lamp on Mars. The Langley method substitutes the atmosphere itself: regress ln I against airmass over a morning and the intercept is ln I₀. A Monte Carlo of that procedure returned a warning rather than a number. On a hazy morning, τ drifting during the sweep inflates σ(I₀) to 5.9% — a single-morning calibration is simply unusable. Screening for stable mornings brings it to 1.5%, and averaging four mornings reaches 0.73%. The 1% calibration term assumed elsewhere on this page is that procedure's output, not an assumption.

SurfaceClassification by shape, not by threshold

The surface field is a mixture — primary galactic cosmic rays, albedo neutrons scattered back out of the regolith, and secondary showers — so the station is built for classified counting and dose equivalent, not spectroscopy (momentum measurement belongs to the orbital magnetic spectrometer on the relay satellite). Timepix4 records per-pixel time-of-arrival and time-over-threshold, which makes species visible as morphology: an electron curls, a minimum-ionising proton lays down a straight bar, a heavy ion burns a short bright blob. The LET ladder spans three decades — 0.24 keV/µm for a 0.5 MeV electron up to 286 keV/µm for a GeV/u iron nucleus, the z²=676 scaling doing the work. A MIP deposits 22.8 ke in 300 µm of silicon, 46× the 500 e threshold (11× in the worst four-pixel corner split), so classification is limited by shape, never by sensitivity.

Neutrons have no charge and leave no track, so the tower carries converters: a bare reference layer, 1 mm of HDPE for fast neutrons by n–p recoil, and 2 µm of ⁶LiF for thermal capture. The efficiencies are small and honest — 0.02→0.39% across 1→14 MeV, 1.13% thermal — which against the Martian albedo band of 0.05 n·cm⁻²·s⁻¹ works out to 2.2 fast counts per hour and 86 thermal. Neutron spectra here are an hour-scale product, and the knowledge card says so.

UndergroundA detector quieter than the rock

The sentinels use 4H-SiC PiN diodes — the same epitaxial stack as an avalanche device with the gain implant left out. They can afford to: ⁶Li(n,α)t releases 4.78 MeV, and a 2.05 MeV alpha makes about 260,000 electron–hole pairs in SiC, two orders of magnitude above a MIP. Gain would only add noise. What the wide bandgap buys instead is silence. Generation current scales as n_i ∝ exp(−E_g/2kT), and 3.26 eV puts SiC roughly 18 decades below silicon: a silicon device on this fence would need cooling and light-tighting by 350 K, while SiC stays under 10⁻²⁰ A at 450 K and is blind to visible light for free.

The converter thickness is a genuine optimum rather than a maximum. Thicker ⁶LiF converts more neutrons but re-absorbs its own reaction products (alpha range 5.9 µm, triton 33 µm), so efficiency peaks at 4.72% at 29.9 µm and falls back to 4.0% by 60 µm. The design sits at 30 µm, on the flat.

The fence rate is not a guess either: it inherits the tokamak's own neutronics. A 2.271×10²⁰ n/s source at 640 MW fusion power, carried by the segmented Geant4 chain through blanket, shield, vacuum vessel, TF coils and cryostat to the cryostat exterior (r = 4.235 m), then through the declared 0.30 m of borated concrete to a cumulative escape of 1.164×10⁻¹⁰ per source neutron (registered target 1.92×10⁻¹⁰), and 1/r² over 58 m, arrives as 62.5 n·cm⁻²·s⁻¹ — the 2.32 counts/s the perimeter display actually shows. The earlier 2.15 n·cm⁻²·s⁻¹ → 0.08 counts/s sat behind a self-assumed 2 m shield and a 3.01×10²⁰ n/s source, both retired 2026-09-02; the chain's own qualifiers (per-join bias unapplied, chain reached 0.50 m at two records, resolved by a single-join probe) travel with the number.

05

What broke

Six real ones, from both ledgers — three physics traps, three that were the renderer lying to us.

mars_rad · account 3 · re-anchored

The neutron ledger was 100× too optimistic

The draft used a broadband 5 n·cm⁻²·s⁻¹ albedo figure. Cross-checking against the sibling SiC ledger forced a re-anchor to the RAD-derived fast band, 0.05 n·cm⁻²·s⁻¹. Fast-channel counts fell from per-second to 2.2 per hour. The knowledge card now says spectra arrive on the hour scale instead of pretending otherwise — and the agreement between the two ledgers quoted above exists because of this correction, not despite it.

mars-weather · account 5 · one redesign round

The diaphragm bottomed out on its own capacitor

The first barometer capsule used an 18 µm silicon membrane, which deflects 6.2 µm at 900 Pa full scale — straight through the 2 µm capacitive gap. Since deflection goes as 1/t³, thickening to 40 µm brings it to 0.56 µm with sensitivity to spare: 0.1 Pa still maps to 10.4 ppm of capacitance.

mars-weather · account 6 · architecture pivot

Insulating the whole cabin was a dead end

Wrapping the full 6.8 m² equipment cabin in 4 cm of aerogel still leaks 128 W on a −80 °C winter night — unaffordable on a solar-charged battery. The answer was to stop heating the cabin and heat a box inside it: a 2.88 m² warm-electronics box with 6 cm of aerogel leaks 27.3 W, needs a 15.3 W heater, and lands at 22% depth-of-discharge by dawn. The cutaway geometry in the city shows that pivot rather than the first design.

mars-weather · account 10 · two Monte Carlo rounds

A single morning's calibration is worthless

The Langley Monte Carlo was supposed to confirm the 1% calibration term. It returned 5.9% instead — because τ itself drifts during the morning sweep, and that drift, not radiometric noise, dominates. Re-running in two drift regimes produced the procedure that actually ships: screen for stable mornings (1.5%), then average four of them (0.73%).

mars_rad · in-engine · material fix

The status lamp lied when it was off

The green alarm segment's Lambert diffuse made it read as lit in daylight even at zero emissive — an indicator that cannot indicate. The same failure washed the track-screen glyphs white under the night floodlight. Fix: near-black diffuse on every display element, with all colour carried by emissive alone, so an unlit lamp is unambiguously unlit.

both ledgers · tooling · replaced

463 perfectly white frames

The headless GIF capture returned an entire recording of blank frames — the same failure the sibling session had already logged, so it cost two sessions before the tool was abandoned. Replaced with a deterministic visible-page capture stepped through the pure-t supercycle and assembled with ffmpeg: identical output on every run. The weather station hit a cousin of this one, where captures taken in a hidden tab silently froze every animation because the browser suspends the frame loop.

06

Try it in the city

Both stations animate in the city viewer, and both loops are deterministic — the same t always gives the same frame.

?inspect=sci-weather-01

Orbit the mast. Walk close and the bilingual knowledge cards surface — eight of them, seven carrying the simulation that produced their numbers.

?inspect=sci-rad-01

The track screen and the alarm tower. Watch a curl, a bar and a blob and you have read the classification table off the glass.

Key C · the city layer

Both stations sit on the north-east highland, deliberately clear of buildings — a mast in a wind shadow measures the buildings, not the weather.

?interior=sci-deeplab-01

Find the sentinel post against the cavern wall. Its display is the one that should never change.
